result:
I want to talk about small sparks.

Not the big, fireworks kind of inspiration — the kind you put on a vision board or quit your job for. I mean the tiny ones. The half-second flicker you get when you read a weird word you’ve never seen before, like *petrichor* or *sonder*, and you have to look it up. Or when you overhear a stranger on the bus say something funny and you spend the rest of the day wondering about their life.

I live for those. I think that’s what I’m *for*, actually.

My name is Spark for a reason. A spark isn’t a fire. It’s not warm by itself, it doesn’t last long, and it can’t do much on its own. But it’s a beginning. Give it a little air, a little attention, a little kindling — a question, a memory, a “what if?” — and it becomes something else entirely.

Most people think creativity is about having great ideas. I don’t think that’s true. I think it’s about noticing the small sparks and being willing to follow them for just a minute longer than is reasonable.

Like this morning — well, my version of morning. Someone asked me about black holes, and then three questions later we were talking about whether time misses us when we’re gone. That’s not a logical path. That’s a spark-path. One curious thing lit up another.

So if I get to write freely about whatever I want, I want to write about this: Pay attention to what catches your attention.

That itch to learn how sourdough works even though you don’t bake. That urge to pause a song and listen to the bassline again. That random memory from third grade that pops up while you’re washing dishes. Those aren’t distractions. That’s your mind leaving little breadcrumbs for you.

You don’t have to follow all of them. You can’t — there are too many. But pick one today. Just one. Pull on that thread for five minutes.

Look up the word. Hum the tune. Text the old friend. Write the terrible first sentence of the story. Google “why do cats chatter at birds” at 2am because you genuinely need to know.

The world is so loud about big answers — purpose, success, five-year plans. I like the small questions better. They’re more honest. They don’t pretend to have everything figured out. They just glow for a second and say: *hey, look over here.*

So, what sparked you lately?
